title: Why Vertical Lines Have Undefined Slope

scenes.title: What is the slope through (3, −2) and (3, 7)?
body: Both points have the same x-value.
scenes.narration: Find the slope of the line through three, negative two and three, seven. Both points have the same x-value. This is exactly where students often mix up zero slope and undefined slope. The answer is not zero. Here is the idea.

scenes.title: Slope measures vertical change per horizontal change
body: m = change in y ÷ change in x
The denominator tells us how far we moved sideways.
scenes.narration: Slope is vertical change divided by horizontal change. The denominator matters because it tells us how much x changed. On a vertical line, x does not change at all, even though y does. So the horizontal change is zero.

scenes.title: Now calculate it carefully
scenes.narration: Now calculate. The change in y is seven minus negative two, which is nine. The change in x is three minus three, which is zero. That gives nine divided by zero. Division by zero has no real-number value, so the slope is undefined.

scenes.title: Why undefined is NOT the same as zero
body: Zero slope: Δy = 0 and Δx ≠ 0 → horizontal line.
scenes.narration: Notice the difference. Zero slope happens when the numerator is zero: y does not change, so the line is horizontal. Undefined slope happens when the denominator is zero: x does not change, so the line is vertical. Mixing up numerator and denominator is the common mistake.

scenes.title: Quick check: recognize the structure first
body: Same x-coordinate for two distinct points → vertical line.
Equation form: x = a → undefined slope.
scenes.narration: So before doing any arithmetic, look at the x-values. If two distinct points have the same x-coordinate, the line is vertical, its equation looks like x equals a number, and its slope is undefined. That is the idea to remember, not just a formula.
